newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senators hear of Indonesian cash to Democrats.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators hear of Indonesian cash to Democrats.

text.p: A U.S. Senate committee investigating campaign finance abuses heard evidence on Tuesday that an Indonesian company funneled money to President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee opened its second week of business by hearing testimony and examining documents showing that in 1992 the wealthy Indonesian company, the Lippo Group, reimbursed an American subsidiary for a $50,000 contribution to the Democratic National Committee in August 1992.

The reimbursement was sought by John Huang, who was then an executive of the Los Angeles-based subsidiary, Hip Hing Holdings, a money-losing operation whose sole asset was a parking lot worth several million dollars.

Huang, a former Commerce Department official who Clinton and others pushed to have hired as a DNC fund-raiser for the 1996 election cycle, is accused by Republicans of raising hundreds of thousands of dollars in illegal political contributions, allegedly of foreign origin.

The 16-member committee chaired by Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson heard from a former Hip Hing officer, Juliana Utomo, who worked for Huang and said she signed the $50,000 check for the DNC at the request of Huang or another officer without knowing what the DNC was.

Days later, Huang sent a request to Lippo's Jakarta headquarters seeking a wire transfer of $146,500. It specifically cited the $50,000 to the DNC Victory Fund as an expense for which reimbursement was sought.

"There's a pretty clear document here requesting a reimbursement for a $50,000 donation to the DNC Victory Fund, which certainly looks like the movement of foreign money into an American campaign in 1992," observed Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat.
A subsequent income statement for Hip Hing Holdings for the year ending Dec. 31, 1992, showed Hig Hing lost $482,000 that year.

The committee also produced documentation, affirmed by Utomo, showing that upon hearing in June 1994 that Huang was to go to work at the Commerce Department, Lippo paid Huang a severance bonus of $425,000, plus $17,500 for unpaid vacation and $25,000 for a Mercedes Benz.
Republicans contend Huang was a lackey of the Lippo Group's controlling family, the Riadys, and remained so while working for Clinton's Commerce Department and at the DNC.

The soft-spoken Utomo said that while she worked with Huang for four or five years before he joined the Commerce Department she never knew what his job was except he approved special expenses when she asked him.

Thompson began his hearings saying that evidence given to the committee indicated China had a plan and may still have a plan to influence U.S. elections. He said the plan was inspired by the perception that Taiwan, which Beijing considers a part of China, had increased its own influence in Congress.
Democrats who believe Thompson is on a partisan witch hunt insisted they had seen the same material as Thompson but did not come to the same conclusion.

However, Thompson was backed on Tuesday by Lieberman after CIA and FBI officials briefed committee members privately on Monday. He said the evidence supported Thompson's contention that China had hatched a plan to influence congressional elections, although he said it was not clear whether this also applied to the 1996 presidential campaign.
"Whether that conclusion can be proved either in this committee, in its hearings, or in a court of law, remains to be seen," Lieberman said.

Trying to add fuel to Thompson's argument, the committee called Richard Hampson, a private investigator who testified said the multi-billion-dollar confederation of companies known as the Lippo Group in recent years had "shifted its strategic center" from Indonesia to China.
